extracted.intended_audience: educational institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, and legal practitioners implementing or interpreting Title IX
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and definitional criteria for identifying and responding to sex-based harassment under the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations, including quid pro quo, hostile environment, and related procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct must be 'on the basis of sex'
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex-based harassment prohibited by this part must be conduct that is “on the basis of sex.” The definition states that the conduct prohibited must be “on the basis of sex,” and includes sexual harassment and harassment on the bases described in § 106.10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhering to statutory language, conduct need not be sexual in nature to be sex-based. The Department declined to remove the reference to § 106.10 because it clarifies the scope of discrimination on the basis of sex. The introductory regulatory language states sex-based harassment “means sexual harassment and other harassment on the basis of sex, including on the bases described in § 106.10.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-category requirement (quid pro quo, hostile environment, specific offenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute prohibited sex-based harassment, the sexual harassment or harassment on the bases described in § 106.10 must satisfy one or more of the three categories: quid pro quo, hostile environment, or specific offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations tie the three categories directly to the definition to clarify scope; the Department declined to further define 'harassment' beyond these categories in the regulatory text because the definition (including the three categories) is deemed sufficiently clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile environment—elemental standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile environment sex-based harassment must be unwelcome, sex-based, and subjectively and objectively offensive, and so severe or pervasive that the conduct results in a limitation or denial of a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition is aimed at discriminatory conduct—conduct that is unwelcome as well as sex-based, and that has an impact far greater than being merely bothersome or offensive. The regulations require both subjective and objective offensiveness and a severity/pervasiveness threshold (the final rule uses 'severe or pervasive').

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of circumstances and enumerated factors for hostile environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of whether a hostile environment exists requires a contextual consideration of the totality of the circumstances and consideration of enumerated factors specified in the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations enumerate factors that a recipient must, at a minimum, consider in determining whether a hostile environment has been created (the preamble notes prior guidance was less specific). Courts have long accepted subjective/objective standards and totality analyses in harassment contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with Davis standard (severity threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final definition is consistent with Davis because it requires contextual, totality-of-circumstances consideration of conduct that implicates access to educational benefits; however, it requires that conduct be 'subjectively and objectively offensive' and 'severe or pervasive' (using OR), rather than Davis's phrasing 'severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains this difference as appropriate for administrative enforcement (where educational access is the goal) as opposed to private damages claims; the rule therefore adopts guardrails that courts identified as necessary to avoid vagueness/overbreadth problems (e.g., objective and subjective qualifiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid pro quo definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Quid pro quo sex-based harassment covers any employee, agent, or other person authorized by the recipient to provide an aid, benefit, or service under the recipient's education program or activity, and includes both explicit and implied conditioning of an aid, benefit, or service on a person's participation in sexual conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition retains 'unwelcome' as an element (the Department declined to remove it). Acquiescence or failure to complain does not mean the conduct was welcome. Student leaders are not presumptively 'authorized' persons (students are generally beneficiaries), but if a student occupies a position authorizing provision of an aid/benefit/service they could be covered. Quid pro quo can include threats of detriment even if the threat is not carried out, and covers non-academic aspects (e.g., extracurriculars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online conduct included
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile environment and other covered sex-based harassment may occur online in addition to in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explicitly notes that covered conduct could occur online; online incidents are evaluated under the same definitional requirements (unwelcome, sex-based, subjective/objective offensiveness, severity/pervasiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope includes harassment based on sex stereotypes, characteristics, pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination encompasses, at a minimum, discrimination against an individual based on sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All these classifications depend, at least in part, on consideration of a person's sex and therefore fall within the scope of 'on the basis of sex' for sex-based harassment analysis; the Department declined calls to narrow this scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance-procedure evidence and false-allegation safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must evaluate complaints of sex-based harassment based on all relevant not otherwise impermissible evidence; provide each party equal opportunity to access relevant evidence or an accurate description of it; provide a process to question parties and witnesses when credibility is in dispute; take reasonable steps to protect privacy; and may discipline individuals who make false statements provided discipline is not imposed solely based on the recipient's determination whether sex discrimination occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific regulatory cross-references include § 106.45(b)(6) and (7) (evaluate based on all relevant not otherwise impermissible evidence), § 106.45(f)(4) (access to evidence or accurate description), § 106.45(g) (process to question parties/witnesses), § 106.45(b)(5) (privacy protections), and § 106.45(h)(5) (discipline for false statements with limitations). These safeguards are articulated as protections against false allegations and to ensure due process and consistent enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment considerations and limits on regulating speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of hostile environment sex-based harassment was crafted with First Amendment concerns in mind: the Department requires unwelcome, sex-based conduct that is subjectively and objectively offensive and so severe or pervasive as to limit or deny participation, thereby targeting discriminatory conduct rather than protected speech per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that the inclusion of objective and subjective standards and severity/pervasiveness guardrails is intended to protect core protected speech while allowing recipients ample means (other than discipline) to remedy hostile environments. The Department cites case law (e.g., Rowles, DeJohn) supporting that properly narrowed harassment policies can withstand First Amendment and vagueness/overbreadth challenges.
